glosses: to hit, to wound, to wing (a bird)
поразить, сбить выстрелом; ранить или убить из стрелкового оружия

examples.text: Что за охота! подстрелят вас как птицу…
Драка окончилась тем, что офицер подстрелил мужика дробью и добил прикладом.
Лет двадцать пять тому назад он подстрелил сову и где-то на ночлеге сказал эту фразу, но фраза эта почему-то не забылась и, как десятки других, повторяется Яковом Петровичем.

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see bring, down.

examples.text: Dad has brought down a stack of old vinyl records from the attic.

glosses: To make (a ruler or government) lose their position of power.

examples.text: The rebel forces are trying to bring down the president and his government.

glosses: To reduce.

examples.text: The latest budget reforms are intended to bring down the level of inflation.
The causes of income stagnation are varied and lack the political simplicity of calls to bring down the deficit or avert another Wall Street meltdown.

glosses: To humble.
To make (something, especially something flying) fall to the ground, usually by firing a weapon of some kind.

examples.text: He brought down a pheasant with his first shot of the day.
For survival off-the-grid, one should have a gun that can bring down most animals without damaging their meat.

Quinn raised the gun again, wondering if there was anything she could shoot that would buy her more time. Bring down the electric lines overhead? No way could she make a shot like that. Place a call and toss her cellphone at the thing? Not enough time. She substituted the strobe light again, and the ghostlem swatted it out of her hand. She spun, catching herself on the asphalt with stinging fingers, and waited to be jellified from behind.

glosses: To cause (an opponent) to fall after a tackle.

examples.text: Kalinic later saw red for a rash tackle on Paul Scharner before Gabriel Tamas was dismissed for bringing down Diouf.

glosses: To make (someone) feel bad emotionally.

examples.text: The news of his death brought her down.
I went to a shrink, to analyze my dreams / He said it's lack of sex that's bringing me down
Nothing in this world could / Ever bring them down / Yeah, they're invincible / And she's just in the background

glosses: To cause to fall down, e.g. in an accident.

examples.text: From the evidence of witnesses and of the recorded passing times, including the time at which the circuit breakers were tripped when the wires were brought down, the train was travelling at a speed of not less than 70 m.p.h.

glosses: To take (someone) to prison.
To receive a prison sentence.

examples.text: She brought down a five-year bid.

glosses: To incite excitement in (a place or crowd).

examples.text: He brought down the club.

glosses: To calm down (someone).
To stop the effects of intoxication in (someone).
To bring or come down; to descend; to cause to bring or come down.

examples.text: The kitten climbed the tree, but then couldn't get down again.
Don't worry, I got the kitten down.

glosses: To swallow (something).

examples.text: The pill was so large that he couldn't get it down.

glosses: To duck or take cover, usually to avoid harm. Commonly used as a caution or warning in the imperative.

examples.text: With bullets flying, all I could do was get down and pray.

glosses: To concentrate; attend.

examples.text: To get down to the matter at hand.

glosses: To depress; discourage; fatigue.

examples.text: Nothing gets me down so much as a rainy day.

glosses: To relax and enjoy oneself completely; be uninhibited in one's enjoyment.

examples.text: Getting down with a bunch of old friends.
It's Friday, Friday / Gotta get down on Friday / Everybody's lookin' forward to the weekend, weekend

glosses: To dance, particularly without inhibition or restraint, or in a sexually suggestive manner.
To party.
To have sex.

examples.text: She's always willing to get down with him.
And women will not care if Dick finally got down with Jane on Search for Tomorrow
Oh, do a little dance / Make a little love / Get down tonight, get down tonight
You get naked, honey, I'll get down / I'm gonna chase you around

glosses: To leave the table after dining.

examples.text: Mummy, can I get down please?

glosses: To record, most often in writing.

examples.text: Quick, here's a pen, get this down will you, before I forget.
They got the whole song down in an hour.

glosses: To criticise; to be strict towards.

examples.text: Ann is always getting down on these students.

glosses: To use a drug, especially heroin.

examples.text: I can't wait to get home and get down.

glosses: To do or perform well; to make happen; to make a serious effort at doing something.

examples.text: I've got this process down.

glosses: To bet on (something); to place bets; to gamble.

examples.text: He's gotta get down on this sure thing.

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see get, down.
